# Commentaries
# of JOHANN ECK,
<note>Johann Eck (1486–1543) was a powerful German defender of Catholicism and one of the primary intellectual opponents of Martin Luther.</note>
### Most Distinguished Doctor of Arts, Canon Law, and Sacred Theology; Canon of Eichstätt, and Pro-Chancellor of Ingolstadt,
## ON THE MYSTICAL THEOLOGY
## OF ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE.
<note>Dionysius the Areopagite refers to "Pseudo-Dionysius," an influential late 5th-century theologian whose writings on the "unknowability" of God formed the basis of Christian mystical tradition.</note>

->Now reprinted with the greatest diligence.<-

->IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1610.<-

# CONCERNING ST. DIONYSIUS
<note>original: "De D. Dionysio"</note>
## Testimonies of the ancients regarding the Areopagite.
<note>Dionysius was a member of the Athenian high court (the Areopagus) who, according to the Book of Acts, was converted by St. Paul. This page gathers quotes from later saints to prove he was a real and authoritative figure.</note>

---

*Ambrose, Letter 82, Book 10.*
<note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD) was the Bishop of Milan and one of the most influential figures in the early Western Church.</note>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' enclosed in a square border of small scrollwork ornaments.</image-desc>
**S**peaking of those whom *Blessed Paul* converted, he says: "The Apostle did not depart from this group without the gift of grace; for even Dionysius the Areopagite, along with his wife Damaris and many others, believed. Thus, those gatherings of the most learned and eloquent men demonstrated, by the example of those who believed, that they had been conquered by a simple discourse." <note>original: "disputatione"; here referring to Paul's sermon at Mars Hill in Athens.</note> *Similar things are said by Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" (c. 260–339 AD).</note> in the History of the Church, Book 3, Chapter 4; and by Nicephorus in Book 2. The writings of Dionysius are cited by Sophronius of Jerusalem to Sergius of Constantinople; by Pope Agatho to the Emperor Constantine; by Gregory of Nazianzus in his sermon on the Nativity; by John of Damascus in 'On the Faith,' Book 1, Chapter 12; and by others, whom we shall list in the following letter.*

## AND MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## PRINCE AND
### *Lord, Lord Henry, Bishop*
### *of Augsburg,*
### *&c.*
<note>The "Lord Henry" mentioned is likely a successor to Christopher von Stadion. In the mid-to-late 16th century, the Prince-Bishopric of Augsburg was a significant ecclesiastical and territorial power within the Holy Roman Empire.</note>

Although the most celebrated theologian **Johann Eck** <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543) was a prominent German Catholic theologian and a principal intellectual opponent of Martin Luther during the Reformation.</note> long ago dedicated this book by **Blessed Dionysius** on *Mystical Theology* <term>Mystical Theology: A branch of theology focusing on the direct, subjective experience of the divine, often described as "knowing by not-knowing."</term>—illustrated with his most learned commentaries—to the then Bishop of Augsburg, **Christopher von Stadion** of pious memory: nevertheless, I cannot help, Most Reverend and Illustrious Prince, but present this same book, now reprinted, in your name, as if I were planting an ancient garden with a new flower. Although even—
<note>The author uses a botanical metaphor ("planting an ancient garden with a new flower") to describe the act of re-issuing an old text with a new dedication to the current Bishop, suggesting that while the "garden" (the wisdom of Dionysius and Eck) is old, this new edition brings it back to life for a new generation.</note>

<meta>This page continues the formal dedication to Henry, Bishop of Augsburg. It transitions from the mention of the previous edition's dedication to justifying the current one, specifically acknowledging the financial backing of the Fugger family.</meta>

—we already owe much to the generosity, care, and sleepless efforts of the noble and illustrious Lord **Albert Fugger** <note>The Fuggers were a dominant European banking and mercantile family based in Augsburg; Albert Fugger (1516–1575) was a significant patron of learning and a collector of rare manuscripts.</note>, which he devotes to restoring the monuments <note>original: "monimenta," meaning the preserved writings or intellectual legacies</note> of the finest and most especially pious writers. It is because of him that this divine work of *Mystical Theology* <term>Mystical Theology: A branch of Christian theology, attributed here to Dionysius the Areopagite, that seeks to understand the "hidden" or "mystical" nature of God through prayerful experience rather than just logic.</term>, together with its commentary, now sees the light of day once more. I might, therefore, have deservedly dedicated this second edition to him; nevertheless, with his kind permission, it seemed right for good reasons to dedicate it instead to your Highness.

For since the first edition was favored with a patron from among your predecessors, the Princes and Bishops of Augsburg, I judged it most fitting that this second edition—which is certainly not inferior, and perhaps even better than the first—should find no other patron than a Prince, a Bishop, and a leader of Augsburg. It should be granted to none other than the successor of that previous patron after this interval of time: a successor, I say, not only in rank, but also in virtue and learning. **Johann Eck** <note>Johann Eck was a major figure of the Counter-Reformation; he had prepared the earlier edition of this work for Bishop Christopher von Stadion.</note> prophesied and prayed for this for him at the very beginning of his bishopric—

...beginning was marked by deeds worthy of a **Bishop** <term>Bishop: From the Latin "Episcopus," referring to the highest order of ministry in the Christian church, charged with overseeing a diocese.</term>, such as Paul describes: *sober*, *temperate*, *holy*, *blameless*, and *wise*. We congratulate you that these qualities have indeed been divinely granted to you through so many years already spent so laudably in the **Office of Bishop** <term>Episcopate: The tenure or office of a bishop.</term>. He [Eck] hoped that the earlier bishop would truly be an **overseer** <note>original Greek: "ἐπίσκοπον" (episkopon), the root of the word Bishop, literally meaning one who watches over.</note>—that is, one who watches over and cares for the flock, rather than one seeking after their milk and wool <note>A common biblical and classical metaphor: a good shepherd cares for the animals, while a bad one only cares for what he can harvest from them.</note>. We rejoice that you have been and are such a person, and we have no doubt you will continue to be so. He traveled throughout Italy, observing its customs and literary pursuits, so that he might bring back with him experience, wisdom, and expertise in both civil and church law, like so many precious goods; we know that this honor is shared by you as well. But I had intended a recommendation of the book, not a **formal eulogy** <term>Panegyric: A public speech or published text delivered in high praise of a person.</term>, lest I should either offend your modesty or seem to be acting the part of a flatterer rather than a sincere admirer. # DEDICATION

...now that I am first sending [this work] out into the light under my own name as **printer** <term>Printer: In the 16th century, the "typographus" was not just a laborer but often a scholar-publisher who held legal privileges to print specific texts.</term>, I might consecrate these first fruits of my labors to your Most Reverend and Illustrious Highness, as a subject to my most merciful Lord. I do so hoping that, just as you received my predecessor of blessed memory, **Adam Meltzer** <note>Adam Meltzer was a prominent printer in Dillingen who died in 1610. His successor, the author of this dedication, was likely Leonhard Campisch.</note>, into your grace and protection, you might also receive me, who succeeds him in the status of both printer and **husband** <note>It was a common practice in the printing trade for a successor to marry the widow of the previous master printer to ensure the continuity of the printing house and its legal rights.</note>.

Now, as for the excellence of the work itself, **Eck** <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543), a Catholic defender and the primary intellectual opponent of Martin Luther.</note> proclaims it sufficiently in his own **dedicatory preface** <term>Dedicatoria: A formal letter at the start of a book addressing a patron.</term>, so that I do not think anything needs to be added. Furthermore, the author’s own commentaries are recommended among other highly excellent works; for he, the leader of the German theologians of his time, most fiercely defended the **ancestral faith** <note>original: "auitam fidem," referring to the traditional Catholic faith against the changes of the Reformation.</note> against the **innovators** <term>Innovators: A common 16th-century Catholic term for the Protestant Reformers, implying they were changing ancient truths.</term> through his teaching, his public debates, and his scholarly writings. He contended not only with **Andreas Karlstadt** and **Johannes Oecolampadius** <note>Major figures of the Protestant Reformation in Germany and Switzerland.</note>, and other **gods of the lesser nations** <note>original Latin: "minorum gentium dijs." A classical idiom used here sarcastically to describe the Reformers as minor or secondary figures compared to the great leaders of the Church.</note>, but also with

<meta>catchword: himself</meta>

## THE PRINTER

...[against those innovators], clashing hand-to-hand with **Luther** himself—who is like a supreme **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iove summo." A hyperbolic reference comparing Martin Luther to the Roman king of the gods to emphasize his status as the "chief" of the heretics in the author's eyes.</note> to nearly all the heretics of our age—he [Eck] brought back a signal victory with eternal praise from the **Leipzig Disputation** <note>The Leipzig Disputation (1519) was a public debate where Johann Eck successfully maneuvered Luther into admitting that he questioned the authority of Popes and Councils.</note>. This occurred in the year of our Lord 1519, specifically two years after the ill-fated beginnings of the Lutheran heresy, which was undertaken under **bad omens** <note>original: "malis avibus," literally "with evil birds," an ancient Roman idiom for an enterprise started with poor prospects or a curse.</note> in the year 1517. It was in that same year that Eck composed these commentaries of which I speak.

Nor indeed is the hostility between the Lutherans, Calvinists, and their like toward the **Blessed Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 1st-century convert of St. Paul. In the 16th century, the authenticity of the "Dionysian" corpus was a major point of contention between traditionalists and reformers.</note> himself and his **Mystical Theology** <term>Mystica Theologia: A highly influential work on the soul's union with God, historically attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite.</term> and other books any less than the hostility between Luther and Eck. For they even call the origins of Dionysius into doubt; indeed, they expressly affirm him to be *spurious and a forgery*. And lest they seem to speak without witnesses, they bring forward some scholars who they claim are quite venerable due to the "gray hair" <note>original: "canitie," referring to the wisdom or authority of age. The author is being sarcastic, calling these 15th-century scholars "ancient" compared to the 1st-century Dionysius.</note> of many centuries—namely **Gaza** <note>Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a Greek scholar whose work helped trigger the Renaissance.</note>, **Valla** <note>Lorenzo Valla (c. 1407–1457), a humanist who used linguistic analysis to prove certain famous church documents were forgeries.</note>, **Erasmus**, and a few others born only recently. 

On the other hand, [we have] **Gregory the Great**, **Cyril of Alexandria**, **Anastasius of Antioch**, and others, who more than a thousand and... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "pliùs" suggests the next word is "amplius," meaning "more than [a thousand and... years ago]."</note>

<summary>This page describes Johann Eck's intellectual victory over Martin Luther at the Leipzig Disputation and defends the authenticity of Dionysius the Areopagite against critics like Erasmus and Valla.</summary>

# DEDICATION

...[those who] lived more years ago, they say, are too recent for their testimony to be admitted in favor of **Dionysius** and his books.

->*If you were admitted to the sight, my friends, could you hold back your laughter?*<-
<note>original: "Spectatum admissi risum teneatis amici." A famous line from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, used here to mock the supposedly absurd logic of the critics who dismiss ancient witnesses as "too recent."</note>

I say nothing of the very many who, within the thousandth year but many centuries ago, recognized the writings of **Dionysius** as genuine. The adversaries add certain other arguments regarding the style and other such indicators, to which answers have already been given both by others and by **Cardinal Caesar Baronius** <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Vatican librarian and historian who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici* to defend the historical claims of the Catholic Church.</note> in the second volume of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the year of Christ 109; and by **Jacob Gretser**, a theologian of the **Society of Jesus** <note>The Jesuits (Society of Jesus) were the primary intellectual defenders of the Catholic faith during the Counter-Reformation.</note>, in the first volume of his defense of the controversies of **Cardinal Robert Bellarmine** <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621) was one of the most important cardinals of the Catholic Reformation, known for his systematic defenses of Church doctrine.</note>, book 4, chapter 7. However, because these volumes are massive and are not at hand for many people, it is pleasing to transfer a few points from them, condensed into a summary, to this place. In doing so, I aim to confirm the discussion which **Eck** <note>Johann Eck (1486–1543), the author of the commentary this dedication precedes and a famous opponent of Martin Luther.</note> treated in the commentary of this very book, specifically in Proposition 3 of the Prologue.

<meta>This page continues the printer's defense of the works of Dionysius the Areopagite. # THE PRINTERS.

(:) 5

**Eusebius**, they say, and **Jerome** <note>Eusebius (c. 260–339 AD) is known as the "Father of Church History," and St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the great translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible; both compiled lists of early Christian writers.</note> make no mention of these books, though they otherwise did not omit even the shortest letters of the ancient authors. As if indeed, given the great rarity of manuscript copies before the art of printing had been discovered, it should be such a great wonder that not every author came into the hands of **Eusebius** and **Jerome**! 

Furthermore, why should the silence of **Eusebius** not be viewed as suspect and unworthy of being taken as evidence? After all, as the patron and "standard-bearer" <note>original: *vexillarius*</note> of the **Arians** <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, who claimed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father—a view declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note> (as **Jerome** calls him), he hardly thought it opportune for himself or his faction to publish things that contradicted **Arian** dogmas—even though they were surely present in his library at **Caesarea**, which was packed with all kinds of books. 

And to pass over other examples, he certainly and with malicious intent shrouded in silence the name and writings of **Theognostus** <note>Theognostus of Alexandria was a 3rd-century theologian. His works are now mostly lost, partly because they were not preserved by historians like Eusebius.</note>, that most famous of theologians, simply because he asserted the term **Consubstantial** <note>original: *Consubstantialis*; in Greek, *Homoousios*. This technical term was the crucial "test" of the Nicene Creed, affirming that the Son is of the same essence as the Father.</note>. Yet **Theognostus** did not escape the notice of **St. Athanasius** <note>St. Athanasius the Great was the primary defender of the Trinity against Arianism in the 4th century.</note>, who frequently cites him with honor. Nor am I the first to raise this point; long ago **St. Maximus the monk** <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), a defender of orthodoxy who wrote influential "Scholia" or commentaries on the works of Dionysius.</note>, a strenuous...

<meta>catchword: pro</meta>

<summary>The printer argues that the absence of Dionysius's works from the bibliographies of Eusebius and Jerome is not proof of forgery, suggesting Eusebius suppressed texts that disagreed with his own Arian-leaning theological views.</summary>
<keywords>Eusebius of Caesarea, Saint Jerome, Arianism, Theognostus, Consubstantial, Athanasius, Maximus the Confessor, manuscript rarity, printing press</keywords>

# DEDICATION

<meta>catchword: Ira-</meta>

...as a defender of Catholic truth against the **Monothelites** <note>A 7th-century group who believed Christ had two natures but only one "will" (thelema); this view was declared heretical at the Third Council of Constantinople.</note>, he argued that **Eusebius’s** silence regarding **Dionysius** was a sign of bad faith. As for **Jerome**, it was not his intention to search for authors omitted by **Eusebius**, but rather to compile those he found already listed by **Eusebius**—as he indicates in his *Preface to Dexter*—and to add those whom he found had flourished after **Eusebius’s** death; for it was **Sophronius** <note>Sophronius was a friend of St. Jerome who translated Jerome's *De Viris Illustribus* (On Illustrious Men) into Greek and added his own entries.</note> who added the rest. **Theodore the Presbyter** <note>A 6th-century priest who wrote one of the earliest defenses of the Dionysian writings.</note> refuted this same objection in his *Apology for the Books of St. Dionysius*, which **Photius** <note>Photius (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople, whose *Bibliotheca* preserves summaries of hundreds of lost ancient books.</note> mentions in his *Library*; however, that *Apology* has since been lost.

*The adversaries then wonder why the **Council of Nicaea** <note>The first ecumenical council (325 AD), which established the core of the Christian Creed.</note> made no mention of the books of **Dionysius**, if they were indeed available at that time. Yet, the Council did mention them in Canon 2, as cited in Greek and Latin by **William Morel** <note>Guillaume Morel (1505–1564), a French classical scholar and royal printer.</note> at the beginning of the Greek edition of **Dionysius’s** works; and again in Canon 31, among those canons translated from the Arabic and published by **Turrianus** <note>Francisco Torres (c. 1509–1584), a Jesuit theologian who claimed to have found "lost" canons of Nicaea in Arabic manuscripts.</note>; and even if it had not mentioned them, it would not be a cause for wonder; for why should it have been required to do so?*

<summary>This page addresses why prominent early historians like Eusebius and Jerome might have failed to mention the works of Dionysius, and argues that the Council of Nicaea actually did reference them in certain canons.</summary>

# PRINTERS

**Irenaeus** <note>St. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD), an early Church Father known for his defense of orthodoxy against heresy.</note>, they say, writing in Book 2, chapter 54 *against the **Gnostics*** <note>original: "aduersus Gnosticos"</note>, clearly indicates that the mysteries pertaining to the **Angels** are unknown; yet this fictitious **Dionysius** <note>The author refers to the debate over whether the works were truly written by Dionysius the Areopagite or a later "Pseudo-Dionysius."</note> professes to reveal them in his book on the *Celestial Hierarchy*. He [Irenaeus] certainly denies knowledge, but only of certain things, not all; since even from **Holy Scripture** itself certain facts are established. He therefore challenges the **Gnostics** to reveal other things which are not established from **Scripture** and **Dionysius**; seeing as they themselves had "made" the **Angels**—as they most foolishly professed—according to their own inventions.

**Augustine**, they claim, affirms in his *Enchiridion* <note>A handbook on Christian doctrine written by St. Augustine around 420 AD.</note>, chapter 58, that he does not know the orders of the **Angels** and their differences; which are the **Thrones**, which are the **Dominations**, etc. <note>These are ranks within the traditional nine choirs of angels.</note> But it is no wonder, since the Greek writings of **Dionysius** were more slowly translated into **Latin** <note>original: "Latinitate donata," literally "gifted with Latinity."</note>, and reached the **Latin Fathers** from the **Greeks** at a later date. Hence not even **Gregory the Great**, nearly two hundred years after **Augustine**, read **Dionysius** himself, but rather cited him as he had heard from others; he arranged the choirs of **Angels** in an order somewhat different from that which **Dionysius** handed down...

<meta>catchword: arranged</meta>

<summary>This page addresses objections to the authenticity of Dionysius's writings, explaining that early Church Fathers like Irenaeus and Augustine were either unaware of his specific angelic hierarchies or lacked access to Latin translations of his Greek works.</summary>

# Dedication

Who most eagerly drank in both the hidden mysteries of our Faith and the wisdom of the Perfect from his teachers—the **Divine Apostle Paul**, that storehouse of **Christian Doctrine** who was instructed in the third heaven <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 12:2, where St. Paul describes being caught up to the "third heaven" to receive divine revelations.</note>, and **Saint Hierotheus** <note>Hierotheus is traditionally described by Dionysius as his primary mentor and a fellow convert of St. Paul.</note>. What he drank in, he committed to letters, and he asserted it most firmly even unto the glorious shedding of his blood in noble Martyrdom. Moreover, his most divine writings have always been held most worthy and in the highest honor by every age, both for the grace of their doctrine and for the dignity of their subject matter; by these, he has led even the most learned men into admiration.

And especially that wonderful and preeminent book, **Mystical Theology**, stands more precious than all *Persian* treasures and *Attalic* wealth <note>original: "Persicis gazis & Attalicis opibus." Attalus III of Pergamon was famous in antiquity for his immense wealth, which he bequeathed to the Roman people.</note>, because it is so abundantly filled with so many mysteries and secrets, and the inner shrines <term>inner shrines: original "adytis," referring to the most sacred, private chamber of a temple; here used to describe the deepest, most inaccessible parts of theological study.</term> of a more secret **Theology**, that it cannot easily be grasped by mortals who are not illuminated by divine light.

Although, however, this way of philosophizing about the most blessed first Cause of all through negations and removals <term>negations and removals: This refers to "Apophatic Theology," which approaches God by stating what He is NOT (e.g., God is not finite, not mortal) because the divine essence exceeds human language.</term> was neglected for many years—while theologians (following the custom of the **Parisians** <note>A reference to the University of Paris, the center of Scholasticism, which focused more on logical and systematic analysis.</note>, which is not to be despised) labored day and night with the greatest vigils in explaining the *Sentences* of **Peter Lombard** <note>Peter Lombard (c. 1096–1164) wrote the "Four Books of Sentences," which served as the standard textbook for medieval theology students.</note>—nevertheless, **Negative Theology** has now been revived.

# OF DIONYSIUS THE MOST HOLY 
# Bishop of Athens, the Areopagite, to Ti-
# mothy, the most holy bishop of Ephesus, 
# concerning mystical Theology.

## What is the divine darkness. Chapter 1.

Trinity beyond being <note>original: "ὑπερούσιε" (hyperousios). A central term in this work, meaning something that exists far above the level of created existence or essence.</note>, beyond divinity, and beyond goodness, overseer of the divine wisdom of Christians: guide us toward the beyond-unknowing, beyond-shining, and highest peak of the mystical oracles. There, the simple, absolute, and unchangeable mysteries of theology are veiled within the beyond-light darkness <note>original: "γνόφον" (gnophon). This "divine darkness" refers not to a lack of light, but to a light so blindingly bright that it appears as darkness to human senses.</note> of the hidden-mystic silence. In that deepest gloom, the darkness shines with the greatest clarity; in that which is altogether untouchable and invisible, it overfills the sightless minds with the beyond-beautiful splendors.

This, then, is my prayer. But you, O dear **Timothy**, in your intense exercise concerning mystical contemplations, leave behind both the senses and the activities of the intellect, and all things perceived by the senses and the mind, and all things that are not and all things that are. As far as possible, strain upward in unknowing toward union with Him who is beyond all being and knowledge. For by the unceasing and absolute <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "ἐκστάσει" (ekstasei). Literally "standing outside" oneself; a state of being overwhelmed by the divine.</note> from yourself and all things, in purity, you will be led upward to the ray of the divine darkness that is beyond being, stripping away all things and being released from all.

<summary>This page marks the opening of the "Mystical Theology," beginning with an invocation to the Trinity and an exhortation to Timothy to seek God through "divine darkness." The text introduces the concept of apophatic theology—reaching God by stripping away human concepts and sensory perceptions.</summary>

# Dionysius on the Mystical <note>original: "Διονυσίου περὶ μυστικῆς" (Dionysiou peri mystikēs). This is a shortened title for the treatise "On Mystical Theology."</note>

See to it that none of the uninitiated <note>The "uninitiated" here refers to those who have not been trained in the spiritual discipline of looking beyond the physical world.</note> hear these things. By these I mean those who are entangled in the things that exist, and who imagine that nothing exists "beyond being" <term>transcendentally</term> <note>original: "ὑπερουσίως" (hyperousios). This suggests a way of existing that is superior to and different from the way physical objects or human thoughts exist.</note>, but think they know, by their own human knowledge, Him who has "made darkness His hiding place."

But if the divine initiations <note>The "mystagogia" or process of being led into the mysteries of faith.</note> are beyond such people, what could one say about those even more uninitiated? I mean those who characterize the Cause that lies above all things by the very lowest of existing things, and who say that It is in no way superior to the godless and many-shaped forms they fashion for themselves. On the contrary, they ought to both attribute and <term>affirm</term> <note>original: "καταφάσκειν" (kataphaskein). This refers to "Kataphatic" theology: describing God by what He is (e.g., God is Light, God is Good).</note> all the qualities of existing things to It, as the Cause of all; and yet more properly <term>deny</term> <note>original: "ἀποφάσκειν" (apophaskein). This refers to "Apophatic" theology: describing God by what He is not, because He is so much greater than our words (e.g., God is not "light" in the way we understand it).</note> them all, as It transcends all being. One should not think that the denials are the opposite of the affirmations, but rather that the Cause is far prior to and beyond all privations, being above every negation and affirmation.

Thus, for instance, the divine Bartholomew <note>A reference to the Apostle Bartholomew. Dionysius cites an otherwise unknown, likely apocryphal, writing attributed to him.</note> says that theology is both "much" and "very little," and that the Gospel is "broad and great," and yet again "condensed."

It seems to me that he understood this supernaturally: that the good Cause of all is both "many-worded" and at the same time "brief-spoken," and even "wordless" <note>original: "ἄλογος" (alogos). This can mean both "without a word" and "beyond reason."</note>, since It has neither word nor [intellect]...

# Theology, Chapter 3

...is narrowed <note>continuing from the previous page: "the more we look upward... the more our words are narrowed."</note>; and after the entire ascent is complete, the soul will become totally **speechless** and will be entirely united with the **Unspeakable** <note>original: "τῷ ἀφθέγκτῳ" (to aphthegkto). But why, you ask, do we start from the highest things when making divine **affirmations** <note>original: "θέσεις" (theseis) - positive statements about what God is.</note>, yet start from the lowest things when performing divine **negations** <note>original: "ἀφαιρέσεως" (aphaireseos) - literally a "taking away" or stripping away of attributes.</note>? It is because when we assert the nature of Him who is beyond all assertion, we must begin the positive description with what is most closely related to Him. But when we perform the "taking away" of that which is beyond all "taking away," we must strip away those things which are most distant from Him.

For is He not more "Life" and "Goodness" than He is "air" or "stone"? And is it not more true to say He does not suffer from **hangovers** <note>original: "κραιπαλᾷ." Now open the third book regarding the path of morals, and run through its individual chapters. Since gold is better than silver, so wisdom is better than eloquence; gold is not the price for cheap things, so wisdom is not meant for temporal matters; gold is the gift of Kings, so wisdom ought to be applied to divine and most high things; the stolen gold <note>original: "furtiuum"; a reference to the biblical "despoiling of the Egyptians" (Exodus 12:35-36), where the Israelites took gold from their captors to later use in the Tabernacle.</note> Israel offered to GOD, and so we take wisdom from the Heathens <note>original: "Ethnicis"; referring to non-Christian or pagan philosophers whose logical and rhetorical tools were used by the Church.</note> and use it for the building up of the Church and the praise of GOD.

## *Proposition II.*

<image-desc>Decorative floral drop cap 'T' within a square ornate border.</image-desc>
*The Trinity in divine matters is beyond-substance, beyond-deity, and beyond-goodness: or rather, superior to Deity and goodness.*

Before we explain these points, it seemed appropriate to apply the teaching of Pico the Elder <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to harmonize different schools of thought</note> regarding the reading of the books of the Blessed Father <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>. In his book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & vno"; a treatise exploring the relationship between existence and unity</note>, he says the following:

> *We must take care that we do not make the writings of Dionysius out to be less than they actually are—for they are of the greatest importance. Nor, while we consider everything that we can understand to be a small thing, should we fashion for ourselves dreams and inextricable fictions.*

The most learned Count <note>referring to Pico, the Count of Mirandola</note> warns that the doctrine of the holy Dionysius must be held in honor. Truly, because Dionysius deals in "super-excellent negations" <term>Negations: A method in "apophatic" theology where one describes God by what He is NOT (e.g., "infinite" or "not-finite") because God transcends human language</term>, Pico learnedly instructs us so that no one, by focusing only on pure negations and removals, should think what is understood is worth nothing. Now, let us approach the matter itself. The holy Dionysius invokes the Trinity as the mistress and teacher of this most holy Mystical Theology.

<meta>catchword: Which—</meta>

<summary>This page presents the second proposition of the text, asserting that the Trinity transcends all human concepts of substance, divinity, and goodness. It cites Pico della Mirandola to warn readers against oversimplifying or dismissing these complex "negative" descriptions of the divine.</summary>

--- Page 100 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pseudo-Dionysius’s theology, moving from the advice of Pico della Mirandola on how to read these texts into a specific theological debate about the nature of the Trinity and the "number" of Persons within the Godhead.</meta>

header: Chapter I. Paragraph I. Proposition II.

Although in divine matters there is no material number (the kind that arises from the cutting of a continuous object or the division of an essence), concerning which Augustine says, *in divine matters, cease to count if you do not wish to err* <note>original: "in Diuinis ceſſa numerare, ſi non vis errare"</note>, nevertheless, according to our human way of affirming truths, there is a certain positive number. This is as the Doctors of Common Theology explain in their theological commentaries on the 23rd Distinction of the First Book <note>Referring to the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages; Distinction 23 deals with the names of the Trinity and how we apply numbers to God</note>, arguing against the opinion of Peter Lombard, who posited only a "privative" number <term>Privative number: The idea that saying there are "three" Persons in the Trinity only means they are not "one" in a way that excludes plurality, rather than asserting a positive count as we do with physical objects</term>.

*For there are three who bear witness in heaven* <note>original: "Tres enim ſunt, qui teſtimonium perhibent in coelo"; a citation from the First Epistle of John (5:7), often used to defend the doctrine of the Trinity</note>; for this reason, Dionysius made his beginning with the Trinity, which he then expressed through three "appropriated" terms <term>Appropriations: In theology, assigning a specific attribute (like Wisdom or Power) to one Person of the Trinity, even though the attribute belongs to the whole Godhead, to help human understanding</term>, as Peter of Spain <note>Likely referring to the 13th-century scholar who became Pope John XXI, known for his influential works on logic and theology</note> has clarified here. 

For he affirms that the Trinity is *supersubstantial* (that is, incomparably exceeding every subsisting thing) in relation to the person of the Father, from whom all being comes. He affirms it is *beyond-deity* <note>original: "Superdeam"</note> (that is, exceeding all wisdom and knowledge) in relation to the person of the Son, who is the "art" and wisdom of God the Father. Finally, he affirms it is *beyond-goodness* <note>original: "Superbonam"</note>, that is, infinitely exceeding all goodness;

Truly, it may seem strange to some that, since that Trinity is substance, and God, and good, how it can be said to be **superior to Deity, substance, and goodness?** Although we will reveal this more extensively in the following sections, let us nevertheless touch upon these things briefly, and say that the Trinity is affirmed to be superior to these by way of **excess** <term>Excess (Latin: excessus): In mystical theology, this refers to "transcendence." It suggests that God does not just possess a quality like "goodness," but "exceeds" the very definition of the word</term>: because by an incomparable and infinite excess it exceeds everything intelligible to us through the terms "substance," "Deity," and "goodness." 

For that negation included within superiority has a pregnant affirmation in itself: Just as when we say God is "unnameable," we secretly affirm that he exceeds everything that can be named. Hence, it is more than clear enough here that this superiority does not consist in the reality itself (for how could God be a **super-god**? <note>original: "superdeus"; the author is questioning the literal interpretation of Dionysian language which uses the prefix "super-" to describe God</note>) but that these modes of speaking hold according to our human way of understanding, as was briefly touched upon in the Prologue...

## Proposition IV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring stylized floral and scrollwork designs within a square border.</image-desc>

> *ON the supreme summit of Theology, its simple, absolute, and immutable mysteries are shrouded in the darkness of a silence that teaches in secret.*

However we understand the "summit," within it the mysteries are clothed in a threefold condition, namely: *simple, absolute, and immutable (or unchangeable).* He calls them "simple" because they are the true principles of all knowledge. For indeed, the more primary principles are, the more simple they are, as the Stagirite <note>A common title for the philosopher Aristotle, referring to his birthplace, Stagira.</note> says in the *Posterior Analytics.* <note>original: "Analyticis posterioribus." This is one of Aristotle's foundational works on logic and how we gain certain knowledge.</note> For everything, the further it recedes from the fountainhead of its origin, principle, or Unity, the more it descends into "otherness" and composition <note>In this philosophical sense, "composition" means being made of multiple parts. God is "simple" because He is one and indivisible, whereas physical things are "composed" and therefore more complex and less perfect.</note>, as Plato maintains. Furthermore, they are called "simple" because they are perceived by the simplest power of the mind. For when someone reaches them, there is a brevity of speech <note>original: "pauciloquium." This suggests that as one approaches God, words become unnecessary or inadequate, leading to a "holy silence."</note>. These mysteries are also *absolute*—abstract and without participation <note>In this context, "without participation" means these truths exist independently and are not mixed with or dependent on created things.</note>, having no fellowship with symbols and riddles:

Wherein, that which is clear is obscured; that which is great is narrowed; that which is human is <term>Deified</term> <note>From the Greek "theosis," the process of being transformed by or united with divine nature.</note>; and that which is unknown is more fully unknown. **Reason** unfolds, spreads itself out, and expands everywhere into every corner; the **intellect**, on the other hand, folds into itself and contracts. **Reason** extends those very principles far and wide, applying them to whatever it encounters, and in doing so, it weakens and thins out their clarity and power. ### Chapter 1. Part 11. Proposition 11.

We have rejected the opinion of **Robert Holcot** <note>Robert Holcot (c. 1290–1349) was an English Dominican theologian known for his skeptical and nominalist approach to logic and divine power</note>, because he denied that **non-being** <term>that which does not exist, such as a fictional creature or a void</term> could be understood; we defeated his minor arguments, which were full of fallacies, in that section.

However, O gentle reader, do not let it escape you that **Marsilio Ficino** <note>the famous Florentine philosopher (1433–1499) who led the revival of Neoplatonism in the Renaissance</note> has discovered in this passage that the **One** is **above being** <term>original: "supraens"—a Neoplatonic concept suggesting that the ultimate source of reality (God) is so perfect that He transcends the category of "existence" itself</term>. The **Platonists** affirm this against the opinion of the **Stagyrite** <note>Aristotle, named after his birthplace, Stagira</note>, who asserts in the fourth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*</note> that "being" and "one" are convertible <term>meaning they are essentially the same thing; whatever exists is one, and whatever is one exists</term>. 

**Marsilio**, however, established the **intelligible** <term>that which is capable of being understood by the mind</term> as equal to **being**. But the **One**, which is God, is **above the intelligible** <term>original: "supraintelligibile"</term>; therefore, the One is **above being**. 

But let it be enough to have pointed these things out in passing, since it is not our purpose to settle the clashing opinions of the **Academy** <note>The followers of Plato</note> and the **Lyceum** <note>The followers of Aristotle</note>. Furthermore, the most learned Count **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** <note>A brilliant Renaissance humanist (1463–1494) who wrote "On Being and the One" to try and reconcile the views of Plato and Aristotle</note> discusses this "sword-fight" of ideas at great length in a specific work. 

Nevertheless, I myself side with Aristotle in thinking that the concept of **being** precedes the concept of the **one**; just as the statement "God is" precedes the concept "God is one" in our reasoning. ### Chapter 1. Part II. Proposition II.

[He/This text] teaches us that we must leave behind all things that can be understood <term>original: "intelligibilia"—objects of the mind</term> and all things that can be sensed <term>original: "sensibilia"—physical objects</term>, both those that exist and those that do not. We do this so that we may become capable of receiving the mysteries of GOD without the need for symbols or images. Indeed, he contends entirely that we are led upward in an unknown way <note>original: "ignotè"—this refers to "apophatic" or "negative" theology, where God is known by stripping away what He is not</note>, as we shall make clear in the following Proposition.

And in truth, this way of seeking God is hidden; it is in this that all the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"—referring to non-Christian philosophers like the Greeks and Romans</note> went astray, and all their Philosophy is blind in this regard. They were lost because they did not know what GOD is, and they were ignorant of the correct way to seek Him, as **Nicholas of Cusa** <note>Cusanus (1401–1464) was a German cardinal and philosopher who wrote extensively on "learned ignorance"—the idea that the mind's highest state is knowing its own limits before God</note>, a most learned German, explains at great length in his book *On Seeking God*. It was not for nothing that **Plato** said that *he would marvel if God could be found, and marvel even more if, once found, He could be made known to others.* **Theodorus** <note>likely referring to a Greek commentator or scholar such as Theodoret of Cyrus</note> also quotes him saying, *to have found GOD is not at all easy, and to have understood Him is impossible.*

This is not to be understood as if the will could be directed toward something that is completely unknown; on this point, **Francis de Mayronis** <note>a 14th-century Franciscan philosopher often called the "Master of Abstractions"</note> rightly rejects the views of certain others.

However, something can be loved more distinctly than it is understood, says **Duns Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a hugely influential Franciscan philosopher known as the "Subtle Doctor" for his complex arguments on the nature of being and the will</note>, the more subtle of the Doctors of Common Theology; he confirms this in the First [Book of the Sentences]: *For I distinctly desire Blessedness in particular, which I hope will come to me, though in this life I never distinctly know it.* Thus **Augustine** himself says in the 8th book of *On the Trinity*: *That which is unknown is also loved, provided it is believed.* And **Blessed Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I, known as Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose writings on the "contemplative life" shaped medieval mysticism</note> also says: *From those things which the soul knows, it learns to love the unknown.* Therefore, one must strive toward God through an unknown, transformative, and life-giving love—knowing Him only in darkness and a cloud, as if moving toward the unknown.

**Ecstasy**, however, is a rapture only in the superior portion of the reason or the will, to such an extent that no inferior power can go out into its own operation. **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>original: "Iacobus Faber," a famous French Renaissance humanist and theologian (c. 1455–1536).</note>, a man deeply learned in ancient matters, describes it in the *Life of St. Elizabeth*, saying: *“Ecstasy is a certain withdrawal of the mind, and a kind of calling away from the body, so that some spiritual spectacle may be seen.”*

### Chapter 1. Part II. Proposition IV.

...essence of the cognitive powers, we wish to divide them, and so we shall distinguish them as follows.

First, a **supermundane vision** <note>original: *visio supermundana*; a vision that originates from beyond the physical world but is perceived by the physical senses.</note> can occur through the **senses**. Thus **Moses** saw the burning bush, and **Belshazzar** saw the hand writing upon the wall. 

Second, such a vision occurs beyond nature within the **imagination**, such as the vision of **Isaiah**, of **John** in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, and of **Pharaoh** with the ears of grain and the oxen <note>The dream interpreted by Joseph in Genesis 41.</note>. 

Thirdly, **rapture** <term>raptus: a state of being "seized" or "carried away" by God, where the mind is elevated beyond its natural capacity.</term> or vision occurs in the **intellect** <term>intellectus: the highest faculty of the human soul, capable of understanding spiritual truths.</term> when it is preeminently elevated by God. Thus **Saint Augustine**, in his commentary on Genesis, Book 41, says that **Saint Paul** and **Moses** were "rapt" in this way; and this is fitting, since Moses was the Teacher of the **Synagogue** <note>Representing the Old Testament/Law.</note> and Paul was the Teacher of the **Church**. 

And according to these levels, **three heavens** could be distinguished; it is in this sense that Paul’s rapture into the "third heaven" is understood. However, **Saint Ambrose** <note>A 4th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church.</note> believed that Paul was rapt twice: specifically, to **Paradise** and to the **third heaven**.

### Chapter I. Paragraph III. Proposition V.

The first saying: *All things found in creatures essentially <term>Essentially: Translated from the Latin "quidditativè," referring to the "quiddity" or "what-ness" of a thing—its defining essence.</term> are to be attributed to God virtually and supereminently.* For every cause contains its effect in power <note>original: "in virtute"; in Scholastic logic, this means the cause has the power or "virtue" to produce the effect, even if the cause doesn't look like the effect.</note>: otherwise it would not be capable of producing it, as we showed this in the Prologue of the Commentary on **Aristotle's** *Logic*. But God, by the consensus of all, is the Cause of all things: because *without him nothing was made* <note>original: "sine ipso factum est nihil"; a reference to the Gospel of John 1:3.</note>: and so God contains all things virtually: and for that reason, the affirmations of all things are spoken of him. And there is that wonderful virtual containment, by which a great tree with its fruits and leaves is contained in one small seed.

The second saying: *All things found in creatures are removed from God formally.* <term>Formally: In this context, "formally" (formaliter) means having the specific, limited form that makes a thing what it is in the physical world (e.g., being a "tree" or a "stone").</term> For every creature is by its own nature capable of failing, and is of limited and finite perfection. **GOD** however is of infinite power, infinitely exceeding all creatures. Not only is matter nearly nothing, but every creature in comparison to God is nearly nothing.

### Chapter I. Paragraph III. Proposition V.

Therefore, all perfections found in creatures are truly denied of God. The **Third saying**: *Negations are more proper to God, and truer than affirmations.* For an affirmation about **GOD** is only a virtual connection <term>Virtual connection: Latin *complexio virtualis*. This refers to a statement that is true because God has the power (virtue) to produce a quality, even if He does not possess that quality in a physical or limited way.</term>, but a negation is formal. For that reason, negation will be more powerful: since that which is "formally such" is "simply such," while that which is "virtually such" is "such" only according to an extrinsic designation <term>Extrinsic designation: Latin *extrinseca denominatio*. This occurs when we name something based on its relationship to something else—for example, calling a healthy food "healthy" not because the food itself feels well, but because it produces health in a person.</term>. A formal negation is therefore more proper.

The **Fourth saying**: *Those negations are not opposed to the affirmations.* For a contradiction must be toward the same thing, in the same respect, in the same way, and at the same time, according to the first book of the *Sophistical Refutations* <note>original: "primo Elench."; referring to Aristotle’s *De Sophisticis Elenchis*, a foundational text on logic and fallacies.</note>. But in the present case, affirmation and negation do not occur in the same respect; for which reason they will not be opposites. Just as no learned man would say that two people contradict each other if one affirms that the **Sun** is hot, meaning in its power <note>original: "in virtute"; meaning the sun has the power to create heat.</note>, and the other denies that the **Sun** is hot in its proper form <note>In medieval science, the Sun was often thought to be formally "lucid" rather than "hot," though it possessed the power to heat objects on Earth.</note>.

### Chapter 1, Paragraph IV, Proposition I

Church in distinction 15 <note>Referencing the *Decretum Gelasianum*, a famous early medieval list of authorized and prohibited books. "Distinction 15" refers to its location in Gratian’s later collection of church law.</note>, considers the **Gospels** circulated under the name of **Bartholomew** to be apocryphal <note>Books not accepted as part of the official Bible.</note>. This was not because the Supreme Pontiff rejected the words of Bartholomew—an Apostle worthy of God—but because heretics were publishing impious doctrines under the names of the Apostles.

If, therefore, Bartholomew testified either by word or by writing that **Theology** is both the greatest and the least: it is the **greatest** in its mysteries, yet it is also the **least** and plain according to the literal word. To this, the comparison we read in **Blessed Gregory** <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), a Pope and influential theologian known for his "Moralia in Job."</note> in the *Prologue to Job* is quite similar:

> *Divine speech,* he says, *just as it exercises the wise with mysteries, so for the most part it restores the simple by its surface. It is, so to speak, like a certain river, shallow and deep, in which a lamb may walk and an elephant must swim.* <note>original: "Quasi quidam fluuius est... in quo agnus ambulat, elephas natat." This famous metaphor suggests that the Bible is simple enough for a child (the lamb) to understand, yet deep enough for the greatest scholar (the elephant) to never find the bottom.</note>

So it happens regarding our **Faith**. If it is viewed simply, it is easy and possible; but if it is investigated subtly, it is impassable, transcending both sense and reason, according to that saying of the Prophet in the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. The quote is from Isaiah 7:9.</note>: *Unless you believe, you shall not understa[nd...]*

...ing. Or certainly, **Theology** is the "greatest" because of all the assertions made concerning God; and again, it is the "least," since God, being unnamable, cannot be expressed by any name. Again, it could be called the greatest in an "unfolded" sense <note>original: *explicativè*. This refers to the process of detailing and expanding upon divine attributes.</note>, but the least in an "enfolded" sense <note>original: *complicativè*. This describes how all complex truths are contained simply and densely within God's unity.</note>.

Or, to speak closer to the mind of the Holy Father: **Symbolic Theology** is the greatest, for it uses many words; while **Mystical Theology** is the least, for it uses very very few words. Likewise, Theology can be called the greatest in its power <term>virtute: in this context, the inherent efficacy or "virtue" of a thing</term>, yet the least in its words. 

For just as a small gem or a tiny pebble is "enfolded" within a small circumference, yet when you begin to "unfold" its power, something great is revealed. A small tool sometimes offers many advantages if its uses are fully detailed; the same happens with divine discourse.

### Chapter I. Paragraph IV. Proposition II.

The **Gospel**, which contains the life of **JESUS** the Savior and his **Sacraments** <term>Sacramenta: here used in the broader sense of "sacred mysteries" or divine secrets, rather than just the specific ritual sacraments</term>, is said to be both broad and concise. Just as in the person of Christ, many similar contradictions are found due to the diversity of his natures. For in him is the immensity of Divinity and the smallness of humanity. These were brought together into one by **David**:
> *the rich and the poor together as one*. <note>original: *simul in vnum diues & pauper*. From Psalm 49:2. The author interprets the "rich" as Christ’s divinity and the "poor" as his humanity.</note>

We find another similar contradiction in the Gospel law, which is both easy and difficult. For it is arduous for the wicked because of the loftiness of the works it requires and because of human inclination <note>original: *pronitatem*. A technical term for the human tendency toward sin or worldly things</note>, according to that saying of the Royal Prophet <note>King David</note>: 
> *O sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after a lie?* <note>Psalm 4:2</note>

Conversely, the Gospel law is very easy for the good when it is commanded by charity; which, according to **Gregory** <note>St. Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and Doctor of the Church</note>, makes all burdens light: 
> *for nothing is heavy to love*. 

So says the Savior:

## Proposition V.

**Abandoning sounds, words, and divine lights, they enter into the darkness. Where He truly is, who is above all things.**

### Chapter I. Paragraph V. Proposition V.

### Chapter 1. Paragraph V. Proposition V.

...things <note>The text likely completes the sentence from the previous page: "Divine things cannot be comprehended."</note> cannot be comprehended; therefore, it is enough that we worship the Divine beings themselves from the heart. Let us take a symbol of this before we move on, which **Cusanus** <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a German philosopher and theologian who explored the relationship between the finite human mind and the infinite God.</note>—unquestionably the greatest **Mystic**—puts forward, and which we have already touched upon in passing.

The physical eye gazes, as it were, for a fleeting moment at the incomprehensibility of the Sun: not because the Sun is not highly visible—since it forces light into our eyes by its own power—but because of its most excellent visibility, it is "comprehensively invisible" <note>The author argues that the Sun is so bright that our eyes cannot "capture" or fully process it; its very brilliance prevents us from seeing it clearly.</note>. 

In the same way, God, who is the highest truth—and truth is the primary object of the intellect—is therefore, absolutely and in Himself, the most **intelligible** <note>Meaning "capable of being understood by the mind."</note> being. Therefore, if it is necessary to approach Him in any way, it must be done through a certain incomprehensible intuition, and as if by way of a momentary **rapture** <note>The original Latin *raptus* suggests a state of being "carried away" or a spiritual ecstasy that transcends normal logic.</note>. 

And thus, transcending both sense and mind, and recognizing the inaccessibility of that light, one [knows/loves] God more perfectly...

## Eck’s Summary

Saint Dionysius prays to be admitted to this sacred darkness, so that he may see God through <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "ignorantiam." The "Negative Way" (apophatic theology), which describes God by what He is NOT, such as "God is not finite."</note>. In affirmations, we begin from the highest things and descend; but in negations, we do the opposite and ascend from the lowest things, so that by the removal of all knowable things...

## Proposition III.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' decorated with foliate patterns within a square frame at the beginning of the proposition statement.</image-desc>
*The order of praising God through affirmations and negations is reversed.*

Once the ways of speaking in <term>Affirmative Theology</term> <note>original: "Theologiæ Affirmatiuæ". Also known as kataphatic theology, this approach seeks to describe God by attributing positive qualities to Him, such as "God is Good."</note> and <term>Negative Theology</term> <note>original: "Theologiæ Negatiuæ". Also known as apophatic theology, this approach describes God by stating what He is not, emphasizing His transcendence beyond human language.</note> are understood, the meaning of this Proposition is easy to grasp. For it depends on two other points declared in our Negative Theology, the first of which is this: *Negations removing more imperfect things from the highest good are truer than others.* The second is: *Affirmations ascribing more perfect things to **GOD** are truer than others ascribing more imperfect things.*

For it is "truer" <note>In this philosophical sense, "truer" refers to how accurately a statement reflects the divine nature. Saying God is not a stone is "more true" than saying He is not a substance because a stone is further removed from His perfection.</note> to say that God is not a stone than that He is not a substance; likewise, it is more truly said of God that He is not a sensing being than that He is not an intelligent being. Conversely, it is more truly asserted of **GOD** that He is intelligence than that He is a

### Proposition III.

*The order of praising God through affirmations and negations is opposite.*

Having established the ways of speaking in **Affirmative Theology** and **Negative Theology** <note>Affirmative theology seeks to describe God by what He is (e.g., "God is Wise"), while Negative theology describes Him by what He is NOT (e.g., "God is not finite") to preserve His mystery.</note>, the understanding of this Proposition is easy; for it depends on two other principles declared in our "Negative Theology":

The first is this: *Negations that remove more imperfect things from the highest good are truer than others.* 
The second: *Affirmations that attribute more perfect things to God are truer than others that attribute more imperfect things.*

For it is "truer" to say that **GOD** is not a stone than to say He is not a <term>substance</term> <note>original: "substantiam". In this philosophical context, a substance is a fundamental being that exists in itself, whereas a stone is a specific, limited physical object.</note>. Again, it is more truly said of God that He is not "sensing" <note>original: "sentiens". This refers to the physical capacity of sensory perception (sight, touch), which implies having a physical body.</note> than that He is not "intelligent."

On the other hand, it is more truly asserted of **GOD** that He is <term>intelligence</term> <note>original: "intelligentia". This refers to the highest form of spiritual understanding, which is more appropriate to God's nature than lower forms of existence.</note> than that He is...

<summary>This page outlines a fundamental rule of mystical theology: when using negative descriptions of God, one should start by denying the lowest things (like being a stone), but when using positive descriptions, one should use the highest possible concepts (like intelligence).</summary>

## Chapter II. Proposition III.

...soul: and it is more truly said of Him that He is **knowing**, than that He is **vegetating** <note>original: "vegetans". In medieval philosophy, this refers to the "vegetative" level of life—basic growth and nutrition shared with plants—which is the lowest level of life.</note>, or a stone. From this comes the reason why the most blessed Father <note>Referring to St. Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose works on "The Divine Names" defined how the Church talked about God's nature.</note> called the first Cause of all things **supersubstantial** <note>original: "supersubstantialem". This term implies that God is not just "a being" (substance) among others, but is "above" or "beyond" the very category of being itself.</note>, and not "super-accidental," even though He is superior to both <term>substance</term> and <term>accident</term> <note>In this philosophical framework, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself (like a person), while an "accident" is a quality that only exists within a substance (like the color of their hair). To be "above substance" is a far higher claim than to be "above accidents."</note>. Truly, it is a greater thing to excel beyond substance than beyond accident; therefore, he wished to name **GOD** from the greater and more perfect category. 

In the process of **negation** <note>Negative or "Apophatic" theology, which describes God by what He is NOT (e.g., God is not limited).</note>, therefore, one must begin from the lowest and most recent things, and from there a step-by-step ascent is made to the highest—as we will explain more broadly at the end of Chapter 3. However, in **affirmations** <note>original: "positionibus". Also known as Positive or "Kataphatic" theology, which describes God by attributing perfections to Him (e.g., God is Wise).</note>, we begin from the first and highest things and descend through the middle to the extremes, just as St. Dionysius arranged the affirmations in his book *On the Divine Names*. 

Let us briefly place the matter before your eyes, so that it may be more faithfully impressed upon the minds of the listeners; although we do not wish to set down every divine thing here.

...[Cusa]nus, or otherwise a navigator <note>original: "nauita"; likely a metaphorical reference to a theological "explorer" or a specific scholar whose name ends in "-nus."</note>, who here judged that *Saint Dionysius* intended to establish a descent in affirmations by way of division from the more general: as, *if God is <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"; the most basic category of existence.</note>, and not an <term>accident</term> <note>original: "accidẽs"; in Aristotelian logic, a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing.</note>, He is therefore a substance. Since the natural process begins from the things better known <note>original: "notioribus 1. ### Chapter 11. Proposition IV.

It is clearer than the sun. Once again, these <term>ablations</term> <note>original: "ablationes"; the process of "taking away" or stripping away concepts from God to reach a higher understanding.</note> are not only made in regards to corporeal things; rather, everything must be removed and denied of God. And thus, through the removal of all things, we enter into the **sacred darkness** and recognize the hidden truth. This is what Francis de Mayronnes <note>original: "Franciscus Maronis"; a 14th-century Franciscan theologian known as the "Master of Abstractions."</note> did not notice, as becomes more clearly evident in chapter 5.

For just as every creature participates in **being** from God, so too does it participate in **truth**, so that divine truth lies hidden and veiled in all things, and yet in all things it shines back in its own way. And from the fact that it shines back, we receive symbols, and <term>Symbolic Theology</term> <note>A branch of theology that uses material images and metaphors to describe the divine.</note> is derived. But from the fact that it is hidden—since truly *God is a hidden God* <note>original: "Deus absconditus est"; a reference to Isaiah 45:15.</note>—the mysteries of the **super-eminent light** are drawn forth, and <term>Mystical Theology</term> <note>The study of God through direct, experiential union that transcends intellectual concepts.</note> is produced.

For whatever we understand positively about God are certain "shining-backs" or divine participations; in themselves, they are surely hidden. Whence the most holy Father [Dionysius] elegantly intended in his book *On the Divine Names*: *Divine things are known only by participation; for how they might be in their own principle and their own seat, no <note>The text cuts off here and continues on the next page.</note>*

Chapter II. Proposition IV.

...if it were manifest <note>original: "festum," likely a transcription of "manifestum"</note> to men, it would not be possible for them to find divine things. ### Chapter III. Part 1. Proposition 1.

[He] colors [the essence] with many disguises <note>original: "pluribus fucis colorat"</note>, but it is called "threefold" on account of the plurality of persons; and this is how St. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian</note> is to be understood. Although, as a rule and by the strict meaning of words, a numerical term added to an essential term <note>a noun referring to God’s nature, such as "Deity" or "Essence"</note> counts the essence itself. This was noted by Pierre d'Ailly <note>Petrus Cameracensis (1351–1420), a French theologian and cardinal</note> in the sixth question of his first book, following the standard teachings on the twenty-fourth distinction of the First Book [of the Sentences]. 

For this reason, Stephen Brulefer <note>Stephanus Prulifer (d. c. 1497), a Franciscan theologian known for his critiques of Thomism</note> reproaches St. Thomas [Aquinas] because, in the hymn for the Body of Christ <note>the feast of Corpus Christi</note> which begins *At these holy solemnities* <note>original: "sacris solemnijs"</note>, he concluded at the end: *Thee, threefold Deity and one, we pray* <note>original: "Te trina Deitas vnaq; poscimus"</note>. But since St. Aquinas was not unaware of the logic behind these terms, as is evident from his commentaries on that passage, we believe he should be interpreted charitably. In the same way, we have applied a more favorable meaning to St. Dionysius than his words might suggest at first glance.

### Chapter III. Part 1. Proposition II.

...the person is not in itself through circumincession <note>original: *circumincessionem*; the theological concept where the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit "interpenetrate" or exist within one another while remaining distinct</note>, but by another reason of origin. Saint Dionysius <note>Refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose writings on the divine names and celestial hierarchies were central to medieval thought</note> meant this significantly when he said they remained in one another by *co-eternal budding* <note>original: *coeterna pullulatione*; a metaphor describing the persons of the Trinity arising together eternally like buds from a single source</note> (that is, by their origin), so that the Holy Father most learnedly intends the origin of consubstantiality <note>The doctrine that the three persons of the Trinity share the same "substance" or essence</note> to be the reason for circumincession.

From this you may infer that the Greeks <note>The Eastern Orthodox Church</note> (provided they are willing to agree with Dionysius) must confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: just as they finally agreed, when matters were desperate, at the Council of Florence <note>The Council of Florence (1431–1449) was a major attempt to reconcile the Great Schism between the Western (Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) churches</note> under Pope Eugenius. For the Holy Spirit is in the Son through circumincession; therefore, this will be by reason of origin and consubstantiality. Otherwise, one person would not be in the other by *co-eternal budding*, as Dionysius says.

From the first, the second originates; from the second together with the first, the third originates. And all these lights will be joined equally, and yet distinct, just as two candles illuminate the space between them distinctly, as is perceived from the distinct shadows. Thus, in the highest unchangeable good, three beneficial lights shine forth: three subsisting persons.*

...was directed toward a greater or lesser **prolixity of words** <note>original: *verborum prolixitatem*; meaning an excessive length or wordiness in speech.</note>. Perhaps you ask: what is the reason why we begin **affirmations** <note>original: *positiones*; literally "positions," referring to Affirmative Theology, which assigns names to God (e.g., "God is Good").</note> with the most worthy things, and **negations** <note>original: *ablationes*; literally "removals," referring to Negative Theology, which denies that human concepts can describe God (e.g., "God is not a stone").</note> with the lowest things?

This is the reason: because when we wish to designate God—who is above all affirmation—through a positive statement, it is fitting that I attribute the most worthy things and those most closely related to Him first. Therefore, when we wish to designate God through **negation** <note>original: *ablationem*</note>, it is fitting first to remove from Him those things which seem to be furthest from Him. 

For example: **life** or **goodness** is more closely and fittingly attributed to Him than **air** or a **stone**. Conversely, with even more obvious fitness, **drunkenness** <note>original: *crapula*; specifically the sickness or madness following intoxication.</note> and **insanity** are removed from Him before we reach the point of saying He cannot be spoken of or understood.

Chapter III. Part II.

## Eck’s Summary.

Having carefully inspected the three aforementioned books, it appears that the later ones were wordy <note>original: *multiverbios*; referring to a verbose or lengthy style of writing.</note>, while the earlier ones were of a more contracted speech. This is just as it is in **Mystical Theology** <term>Mystical Theology: A path of spiritual study that seeks a direct, wordless experience of the divine presence.</term>, where we are distanced as much as possible from things that can be perceived by the senses. Finally, in the **darkness** <note>original: *caligine*; often translated as the "Divine Dark" or the "Cloud of Unknowing," where the mind is blinded by the overwhelming light of God.</note>, the scarcity of words eventually gives way to silence, because the mystic is **speechless** <note>original Greek: *alogos*; literally "without word" or "beyond reason."</note>. 

But why is the order reversed when it comes to **affirmations** <note>original: *positionibus*; also called "kataphatic" theology, which describes God by what He is (e.g., God is Good).</note> and **negations** <note>original: *negationibus*; also called "apophatic" theology, which describes God by what He is not (e.g., God is not a stone).</note>? 

The reason is this: because that which is more perfect must be attributed to God. In the case of affirmations, the "higher" things are more perfect; however, in the case of negations, the "lower" things are more perfect. For example, goodness and life are more perfect than air or stone. Conversely, it is a more perfect description of God to say He is "not insane" than to say He is "not understood." Mystical assertions about **GOD** begin from the highest point and descend, whereas negations begin from the lowest depths.

For although **GOD**, above all things, precedes every affirmation and negation according to the opinion of Saint Dionysius <note>original: "Dionysij"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential mystical theologian</note>, yet when it is pleasing to proceed through affirmations (for in these our worship <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latriae"; a technical term for the supreme worship offered to God alone, as opposed to the veneration given to saints</note> and **Religion** consist), one must begin from the highest. This is because that which is highest is more kindred and closer to **GOD**. It is just as nature begins from the heart and the members closest to the heart, and then proceeds to the formation of the outer limbs. For when the most perfect quality is affirmed of **GOD**, the lower qualities that follow are not yet affirmed; therefore, if you attribute other things to **GOD** step-by-step, there will be no redundancy at all. But if you were to begin affirming from the lesser things, you would say too little: since if that which seems lesser is present, then that which is greater will also be present, according to the rules of <term>Topics</term> <note>original: "Topicam"; referring to Aristotle’s *Topics*, a treatise on the art of constructing logical arguments</note>. ### Proposition IV.

The mystic begins his positive statements concerning **God** from the highest point, descending downwards, but begins his removals <note>original: "ablationes"; in theology, this refers to the "way of negation" (apophasis), where one removes human concepts to better understand the divine</note> from the lowest depths.

For although **God**, first of all, precedes every affirmation and negation according to the opinion of **Saint Dionysius** <note>original: "Diui Dionysij"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on "Negative Theology" were foundational for medieval mystics</note>, yet when it is chosen to proceed through affirmations (for in these our worship of <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latriæ"; the highest form of worship or adoration, which the Church teaches is due to God alone</note> and our **Religion** consist), one must begin from the highest point, because that is more akin and closer to **God**. This is just as nature begins from the heart and the limbs closest to the heart, and then proceeds to the forming of the outer limbs.

For when the most perfect thing has been affirmed concerning **God**, the subsequent things have not yet been affirmed; therefore, if you attribute other things to **God** step by step, there will be no redundancy at all. But if you were to begin from the lesser things when making affirmations, you would say very little: since, if that which seems lesser is present, then that which is greater will also be present, according to the rules of <term>Topics</term> <note>original: "Topicam"; a reference to Aristotelian logic, specifically the *Topics*, which provides "places" or methods for constructing arguments</note>. Rightly, therefore, from the highest...

<header>Chapter III. Part II. Proposition IV.</header>

...you will begin by affirming. Conversely, the mystic begins by denying from the lowest depths, because in this way the subsequent things in the ascent have not yet been denied. For if you were to begin denying from the highest and most perfect point, you would have already denied everything at once: for when the superior thing is denied, everything that falls under it is also denied <note>This follows a logical rule: if you deny the existence of a genus (e.g., "animal"), you automatically deny the species under it (e.g., "man"). In theology, if you deny God has "Being" before denying He is a "Stone," the latter becomes redundant.</note>; and thus the remaining **negations** would be added in vain. 

Therefore, if you wish to pass through the middle steps correctly and not absurdly (as it is necessary for you to do), you will first affirm the highest things, and conversely, you will correctly deny the lowest things before the others. Just as a sculptor, in carving a statue, first removes the outermost material and then the inner parts closer to the figure, so in negations it is necessary to remove the lowest things furthest from **GOD**, and then those closer to Him. For in the judgment of all, the most perfect things more likely belong to God, while the less perfect are more probably removed from Him: for example, **GOD** is more rightly called "life" (as is attributed to Him in the book *On the Divine Names* <note>original: "de diuinis nominibus"; referring to the influential treatise by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite</note>) than a "stone," as is attributed...

## Proposition I.

*The Cause of all things, existing above all things, is not without substance, life, mind, and reason.*

The doctrine of sacred ignorance <term>sacred ignorance: *sacra ignorantia*, the mystical state where the mind lets go of specific concepts to experience a direct, wordless connection with God</term> is wonderful. Even though in the very next chapter he will deny that God possesses substance, life, mind, and reason, he nevertheless steadfastly affirms here that God is not without substance, life, mind, and reason. I believe this was done for two reasons: first, he wanted to exclude the error <note>the error of thinking God is "lesser" than human attributes like life or intelligence</note>, and second, he wanted to show God's excellence by way of comparison. For he appears to deny these "lesser" goods only so that it may be understood that he is always intending to affirm things that are better in a way that exceeds our understanding. Before I move on from this point, do not let it escape your notice that Peter <margin>Hispanus <note>Peter of Spain (c. 1215–1277), a famous logician and philosopher who later became Pope John XXI</note></margin>

<meta>catchword: Hispanus (referring to Peter of Spain)</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the four stages of Negative Theology and explains the paradox of why God is described as both having and lacking attributes like life and reason. It emphasizes that denying these traits to God is not to diminish Him, but to exalt Him above all human categories.</summary>
