### Chapter IV. Proposition I.

Peter of Spain understood those four attributes mentioned in the Proposition in a negative sense, so much so that those two negatives—*nor without* <note>original: "neq; sine"</note>—do not create a simple affirmation. Rather, he wanted to remove from God anything that is not a substance, such as an accident <term>accident: in medieval philosophy, a quality that is not essential to a thing’s nature, such as a color or a size</term>, anything not living, such as a stone, and anything not rational, such as a brute beast. But we, leaning on the previous opinion, shall explain why he chose to begin in this way. For he did so lest anyone might think, through the removal of everything from God, that the Holy Father <note>Dionysius the Areopagite</note> intended for God not to exist at all. Therefore, before he brings forth his negations of all things regarding God, he puts forward certain affirmations—at least "virtual" ones—even though he is about to immediately deny those same things about God. He does this to show that God is not the kind of substance we imagine, nor the kind of life we know, and so on. Instead, He is beyond-substance, beyond-intellect, and, if I may put it this way, beyond-life. He does this to imply that these are not simple or common negations spoken out of a lack or defect, but are instead "excellent and pregnant" <note>meaning these negations are full of a higher meaning; they deny the word only because the reality is much greater than the word can express</note>.

<sig>T 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: Præ-</meta>

<summary>This page explains that Dionysius uses "negative" language not to suggest God lacks qualities, but to show He possesses them in a way that transcends human definition. It contrasts common negations (lack of a trait) with "pregnant" negations that signify God's overwhelming excellence.</summary>

<keywords>Peter of Spain, Dionysius the Areopagite, Negative Theology, beyond-substance, beyond-intellect, beyond-life, philosophical accidents, divine excellence</keywords>

For this reason, nothing among those things which are created bears a form <note>original: "speciem"</note> through which the creator can be fully reached. But from the magnitude of the form and beauty of the creature, we are raised to that which is infinitely and incomprehensibly beautiful, albeit from a distance and remotely; for an image or a footprint (such as the creature is) is a diminished measure of truth, not an adequate one: for by the very fact that it is an image, it falls short of the truth.

### Chapter IV. Proposition IV.

If you call God wise, you have spoken in a diminished way, for He is also good. If you call Him just, you have spoken in a diminished way, for He is also merciful. If you call Him God <note>original: "θεόν" (*theón*)</note> because He sees all things <note>The author likely refers to an ancient etymological tradition, often cited by thinkers like Clement of Alexandria, linking the Greek word for God (*theos*) to *theasthai*, meaning "to behold" or "to see."</note>, you have spoken in a diminished way because He also creates all things: and so it goes for all other things universally. For God is not a substance that is not also all things; nor is He a wisdom that is not also all things, and so on. Therefore, how could you completely express every perfection by the name of only one perfection? It follows that these particular names of perfections express the "all-perfection" <term>all-perfection: A theological term for the state of possessing every possible excellence or positive quality in its highest, most unified degree.</term> of God in a diminished way.

And I understand that these names apply to Him in a diminished way from their own side <note>meaning from the perspective of the limited human definitions of these words</note>; although they apply to God in an eminent way <term>eminent way: A philosophical concept where God possesses a quality (like "wisdom") in a higher, infinite, and more perfect form than the way humans understand that same quality.</term> from His own side. The entire reason for this is His immensity, as we have often said; and for this reason the most blessed Father <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose work "The Divine Names" founded the tradition of "negative theology."</note> said, *Negations concerning* <unclear>God</unclear> *are true, but affirmations are incompa-* <note>original: "affirmationes verò incompa-". The author likely intends *incomparabiles* (incomparable) or *incompatibiles* (incompatible), but the word is cut off.</note>

This authority is also frequently used by the Doctors of common Theology in <unclear>their works</unclear>. But that with their kind permission...

## Chapter V.

### Eck's Summary <note>original: "Eckii Summarium" — Johannes Eck (1486–1543) was a famous German defender of the Catholic faith. He wrote these summaries to help readers navigate the dense "Mystical Theology" of Pseudo-Dionysius.</note>

Saint Dionysius had removed sensible things <note>original: "sensibilia" — objects we can see, hear, or touch.</note> in the previous chapter; here he also takes away intelligible things <note>original: "intelligibilia" — higher concepts known only to the mind, such as "truth" or "wisdom."</note>, so that he may always proceed upward through the process of denial. And first, he removes those things which pertain to the soul that moves the body; then he removes from **GOD** every mode of understanding. Furthermore, he removes those things which belong to spiritual quantity; again, he separates motion and rest from **GOD**, and distinguishes the degrees and measures of the duration of things. And so that these claims might be more credible, he even removes those attributes which are specifically assigned to God through affirmation <note>In "affirmative theology," we say things like "God is Good." Here, Eck explains that Dionysius even negates these "positive" names to show God is beyond goodness itself.</note>, so that nothing at all remains; he even removes the names of divine concepts themselves.

## Chapter V. Proposition II

I think it is stated far more acutely that St. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, the 5th or 6th-century mystical theologian whose work is the subject of this commentary.</note> has thus far removed corporeal and sensible things from God in Chapter 4, and intelligible things <note>Things that can be understood by the mind but not perceived by the senses.</note> at the beginning of Chapter 5. ### Chapter V. Proposition II

When reading of Alexandria <note>original: "Alexandriam"; the author uses the city as an example of how a name or description does not equal the reality of the thing itself.</note>, you form for yourself a notion of that city which you use to represent it; however, that notion is most unlike the actual city and does not touch upon the truth of the city at all. Likewise, when reading or hearing about St. Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, or **Alexander the Great**, or **Charlemagne** <note>original: "Carolo Magno".</note>, or **Pompey the Great**, one fashions images of them for oneself. Yet if these men were presented in person, one would hardly recognize them, but would rather understand that one’s own notion had wandered far from the truth. How much more, then, does he wander infinitely from the truth who fashions for himself a finite notion of infinite magnitude, which he is unable to reach? For this reason, St. Dionysius removes all these things from God because of their imperfection—not that these things do not belong to God in the highest reality, but because they cannot apply to GOD in the way that we understand them.

But this must also be added: that number, order, and equality are denied of God in this context, not as they are in corporeal <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing as "corporeal things" on the next page.</note>—

### Chapter V. Proposition II.

...things <note>Continuing from the previous page: "as they are in corporeal things."</note> (since in chapter 4 he denied that God is shape, quantity, and so on). But by a more common reasoning, as these attributes also apply to intellectual<gloss>ly</gloss> perceived things, he still denies all those things of GOD through the **way of eminence** <term>via eminentiae: a way of describing God by taking a human virtue or quality to its infinite limit, eventually realizing God transcends the quality entirely</term> and **sacred ignorance** <term>sacra ignoratio: also known as "divine unknowing," the state where the mind moves beyond concepts to encounter God's mystery</term>. 

First, he removes **number**, which we cannot easily understand without making distinctions <note>original: "sine discretione"; the idea that to count things, we must see them as separate, whereas God is an absolute unity.</note>. Then, he takes away **order**, because number without order is merely horror and confusion. "And because in order," says the **Bishop of Lincoln** <note>Linconiensis: referring to Robert Grosseteste (c. 1175–1253), an influential English theologian and scientist who commented extensively on Dionysius.</note>, "there is an arrangement of things equal and unequal," for which reason magnitude, smallness, and equality accompany order; likewise, similarity and dissimilarity belong to the goodness and perfection of order. 

And although order seems to belong to higher realities, he nonetheless rejects **motion**, **standing still**, and **silence** in relation to God. By "standing still," the interpreters understand rest from sensible motion; by "silence," they understand the absence of intellectual motion. All these are denied of GOD by the **way of eminence**, for He is above both sense and intellect.

### Proposition III.

**GOD** is not power, life, substance, eternity, or time; indeed, He is not knowledge, truth, Divinity, goodness, Spirit, Father or Son, nor anything that exists or does not exist.

### Chapter V. Proposition IV.

To the extent that it is understood more hiddenly, to that same extent it seems to approach divine brightness: the term **Theophany** is used here in a much narrower and more restricted sense, which **Maximus** <note>St. Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662), a Byzantine theologian and monk who wrote extensively on the soul's union with God.</note> explains as occurring in this way: *For when the wisdom of God descends through grace into an intellectual nature* <note>In this context, "intellectual nature" refers to rational beings such as humans and angels.</note>, *and makes itself visible, so that the nature itself may in turn ascend through love to the wisdom of God, by which it is attracted and elevated as if by a magnet: and the more God condescends to it and pours Himself into it, the more blessed that nature becomes.* For it is called **Theophany** <note>original: "$\Theta\varepsilon o\Phi\alpha\nu\acute{\iota}\alpha$" (Theophania)</note>, that is, a divine appearance or the appearance of God.

Take this analogy <term>symbolum: here used as a symbolic comparison or illustrative example.</term> so that the matter may be more easily understood. The light of the Sun, in and of itself, is not grasped by the bodily eye because of its overwhelming brilliance; but when solar light is mingled with the air, then it begins to appear and can be perceived by sight; for it is not seen in its pure state, but when mixed with the air, even though the light still remains the dominant element in the air. In the same way God—the **supersubstantial light** <term>lux supersubstantialis: a term meaning light that exists beyond the category of "substance" or created being; a light that is the source of all existence.</term> and truly inaccessible—having been joined to an intellectual nature in a wonderful and new way, begins to appear to it, and [to be seen] <note>The Latin text breaks at "vi-", and the catchword at the bottom of the page is "deri:", completing the word "videri" (to be seen).</note> by it—

### Chapter V. Proposition IV.

...to be seen <note>The text begins with the completion of a word from the previous page, likely "videri" (to be seen).</note>: according to that passage of the Psalms: *In your light we shall see light.* <note>original: "In lumine tuo videbimus lumen." — Psalm 36:9. This verse is a cornerstone of medieval theology, suggesting that humans can only perceive God’s truth through the light God Himself provides.</note> **Aurelius Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian of Western Christianity.</note> seems to have understood this wonderfully in his commentary on those words of **Saint Paul**: *Who was made for us wisdom, etc.* <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 1:30, where Paul describes Christ as the personification of divine wisdom.</note> The Wisdom of the Father, he says, in which and through which all things were made—which is not created but creating—comes to be in our souls by a certain ineffable <term>ineffable: something too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.</term> condescension of His mercy, and joins our intellect to Himself, so that in an ineffable way a certain "composite wisdom" is formed: arising from that Wisdom descending to us and dwelling within us, and from our own understanding being taken up to Him through love and formed within Him.

Nor does that differ from what he left written in his book *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei." This quote comes from Book 22, Chapter 29, where Augustine speculates on the nature of the "spiritual body" after the resurrection.</note>: *Through the bodies,* he says, *which we shall carry, in every body whatsoever we see, and wherever we direct the eyes of our body, we shall contemplate God Himself with transparent clarity.* Weigh these words well, and apply them.

Furthermore, one **Theophany** <note>A manifestation of God to humankind.</note> is more excellent than another, says the same **Maximus**, just as one person will be more blessed than another according to their merits or the grace of God. ### Chapter V. Proposition IV.

We read of Plato repeatedly in the works of <term>Seneca: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero, whose writings were often seen by Christians as compatible with their faith.</term> And <term>Orpheus: a legendary figure of Greek myth, considered by early scholars to be one of the "theologians" of antiquity whose poems contained fragments of divine truth.</term>, a most ancient figure, said regarding this matter that **"God is an infinite eye, because He understands all things."** <note>original: "Deum esse oculum infinitum, quia omnia intelligeret"</note> And <term>Plotinus: the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whose philosophy deeply influenced early Christian views on the nature of God's mind.</term> says, **"All things are certain to God in a manner that exceeds both sense and intellect."** <note>original: "Omnia sunt certa Deo modo quodam sensum & intelligentiam excedente"</note> This knowledge even descended to the Poets, who confessed that God knows all things. Thus <term>Statius: a Roman poet (c. 45–96 AD) whose works were admired in the Middle Ages and Renaissance for their moral and descriptive power.</term> sang in his *Silvae*:

Likewise <term>Lucan: Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet famous for his epic on the Roman Civil War.</term> knew this in the fifth book of the *Pharsalia*, when he wrote:

> What God endures the earth from heaven, holding all the secrets of the eternal course, and conscious of the future world; and ready to reveal Himself to the people. <note>original: "Quis terram cæli patitur, Deus omnia curſus / AEterni ſecreta tenens, Mundiq₃ futuri / Conſcius: ac populu ſeſe proferre paratus"</note>

### Chapter V. Proposition V.

About to complete those matters pertaining to **Mystical Theology** <term>Mystical Theology: a tradition of Christian thought that focuses on the direct, non-intellectual experience of God’s presence, often emphasizing His absolute mystery.</term>, Saint Dionysius here adds the "sum of sums" <note>original: "summam summarum" — meaning the ultimate conclusion or the most essential point.</note>. He had already long ago taught that we cannot reach God through human intelligence; now he concludes that God has neither a name nor a description <note>original: "sermo" — often translated as speech, discourse, or the spoken word.</note>. *For intelligence is the sister of speech, says Hermes; and as the Greeks celebrate in their proverbs, Speech is the Messenger <note>original: "Angelus" — here used in its Greek sense of "messenger" (angelos) rather than a celestial being.</note> of intelligence.* Therefore, he asserts that He who is above all that can be expressed is both ineffable and unnamable, whether we use the highest names, such as "light" and "truth," or the lowest, such as "darkness" and "error." The reason he provides for this is that **GOD** is superior to both **affirmation** and **negation**. Since God is not understood [by finite minds], He can neither be denied nor affirmed, because those acts are the work of the intellect. 

Whence Gregory of Nyssa truly says: *GOD, being beyond every creature, is in Himself comprehended by no intellect; thus He is known to be incomprehensible even in the secrets of nature.* Likewise, Xystus the Pythagorean Philosopher <note>Xystus is the Latinized name for Sextus; his "Enchiridion" or "Handbook" was a collection of ethical and spiritual sayings popular in the early Church.</note> says in his *Handbook*: *The Name*

### Chapter V. Proposition V.

Do not seek the name of **GOD**, for you will not find it; because everything that is called by a name receives that name from something superior <note>The author argues that the one who names a thing must have authority or a higher understanding of it than the thing itself; since nothing is superior to God, no one can truly name Him.</note>, so that one may call out and another may hear. Who, then, is he who has imposed a name upon God? Indeed, "God" is not a name for God, but rather a judgment <note>original: "iudicium" — here meaning a human mental conception or a subjective estimation rather than a definitive label.</note> that we perceive concerning God; therefore, do not seek anything concerning God that is not permitted. Consequently, we must seek a shadowy <note>original: "umbraticam" — referring to knowledge that is like a reflection or a shadow (an "umbra") rather than the direct, blinding light of the source.</note> knowledge of God, since there is no direct knowledge, name, or discourse of Him as He truly is. On this matter, the words of the Spaniard Lazarelus <note>Ludovico Lazzarelli (1440–1500), a famous Renaissance philosopher and poet who sought to reconcile the "Hermetic" writings of ancient Egypt with Christian doctrine.</note> in the *Crater of Hermes* <term>Crater Hermetis: "The Mixing Bowl of Hermes," a dialogue where Lazzarelli explores the transformation of the soul through divine knowledge.</term> are elegant:

> *I do not therefore advise here*, says Lazarelus, *that we ought to know God in such a way that we might distinguish what He is like in His separation from all things, what He is like in the total enclosure of Himself within Himself, or what He is like in that extreme and solitary withdrawal into the deepest recess and darkness of His Divinity, or what His substance might be; for this is far too difficult, indeed impossible. For human intellect cannot ascend so far; for whatever human intelligence defines must necessarily be finite;*

And here you recognize how wondrous mystical wisdom is. Since already with many do- <meta>The text cuts off mid-word ("do-") and continues on the following page.</meta>

For before he [the author] posits that God is superior to both affirmation and negation, he denies that God has any speech or name. This is because everything that is spoken admits to opposition and contrariety; yet nothing of that sort can properly be said of God, since nothing contrary to God could properly exist. For this reason, if God were expressed by the name of "Deity," "Goodness," or "Essence," He would no longer be **ineffable** <term>ineffable: from the Latin *ineffabilis*, meaning that which is beyond words or cannot be described in human language.</term>. Therefore, strictly speaking, nothing is affirmed of the ineffable God; and since He cannot be grasped by the intellect, nothing can likewise be denied of Him.

...[of these] words, it might seem to someone that these are clashing and contradictory; yet they are in no way opposed if you look more deeply into them. For the practitioner of affirmation <note>The "affirmator," or kataphatic theologian, who defines God through positive attributes like "Good," "Just," or "Wise."</note> directs his eye toward the truth which he transfers from created things <note>original: *creaturis*</note> to God, according to the measure of his own human capacity. He clothes and adorns the absolute essence of God with this perfection and others like it, as much as he is able. 

The Mystic, however, recognizing the immensity of **GOD**—how He is incomprehensible and unspeakable—denies that **GOD** is "truth." This is not because God is not the highest and most essential truth, but because the Mystic recognizes that there is something far more excellent and noble in **GOD**, which is Divine Truth. Therefore, he denies and removes from God "truth" as he himself understands it, viewing it as mutilated, imperfect, and infinitely falling short of Divine Truth. Thus, there is a great distance between the ideas that God is above affirmation and negation, and that contradictory opposition coincides in God; for by all names...

# CONCLUSION
## to the Reader.

You have here, honest reader, these commentaries on <term>Mystical Theology</term> <note>A branch of theology focusing on the direct, subjective experience of God and the soul's union with the Divine, often beyond words or logic.</note>. If they have turned out to be more long-winded than you might have desired, consider that, in view of the depth of the mysteries, they are actually quite narrow and brief. I ask that you receive our labor with a grateful spirit, and do not gnaw at it with the **tooth of Theon** <note>original: *Theonino dente*. An ancient Roman idiom referring to harsh, envious, or malicious criticism, named after a famously biting satirist.</note>; for by our night-watches and our sweat—just as in our other works on predestinations, contracts, and excursions <note>original: *excursionibus*. In an academic context, this refers to brief specialized treatises or scholarly digressions on specific points of law or theology.</note>—so also now we have wished to be of use to you. It would be your part, for that reason, not to oppose us, nor to tear apart our reputation. We have laboriously drawn out these more secret mysteries partly from dusty books, which were scarcely legible due to neglect, filth, and decay; partly we were aided by more recent commentaries; and truly, some things we have set forth **by our own effort** <note>original: *nostro marte*. Literally "by our own Mars," a Latin idiom meaning by one's own prowess, courage, or exertion without outside help.</note>, even at some risk. However, I advise you that...

...first, it is a custom in <term>Common Theology</term> <note>Also known as Scholastic or Systematic Theology, the standard academic method of the time based on logic and formal debate.</note> that if one encounters ideas that are very different from its own rules, one should not immediately hiss them off the stage. For these mystical matters must be handled in one way—with a different art and a different mindset—than the decrees of the <term>Sententiaries</term> <note>original: *Sententiarium*. Scholars who specialized in the "Sentences" of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages which emphasized logical categorization.</note>, as I have often warned throughout these commentaries. In these writings, I have also intentionally passed over the squabbles of the Doctors and their clashing arguments with wax-stopped ears in the **manner of Ulysses** <note>original: *Vlysseo more*. Furthermore, by diligent effort, we have often left a subject unexplained in one place, intending for it to be explained more fully in another. We have not only avoided the "makeup" of flowery speech, but have utterly neglected it; *For, as **Manilius** says, the subject itself refuses to be adorned, content simply to be taught.* <note>original: *Ornari enim, vt Manilius ait, res ipſa negat, contenta doceri*. Marcus Manilius was a 1st-century Roman poet; the quote suggests that profound truths are best expressed simply.</note>

In this way, therefore, **Saint Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, the purported author of the foundational texts on mystical theology.</note> has sketched for us the **Unknown God**, just as **Saint Paul** did for the Athenians, in this formal work. This is the God whom man—the "bond of the Universe," placed for that reason on the **Horizon** <note>A philosophical concept viewing humanity as the meeting point or "horizon" between the temporal (physical) and the eternal (spiritual) worlds.</note> of time and eternity—ought to seek, contemplate, and be ineffably united to. However, in all these matters...
